title: Preparing for a Gig: Prep, Backups, Rider & Contingency
skill: Pack a gig kit with prepped USBs, backups, a rider and contingency plans so nothing derails your set.
content:
Treat prep like a pilot's pre-flight

The best DJs are boring backstage because everything that could go wrong has already been solved at home. Your goal is a kit where any single point of failure — a dead USB, a missing adapter, a crashed laptop — costs you zero music. That redundancy is what lets you relax and actually perform.

The USB rule of three

Carry your library on at least two identical, independently exported USB sticks, formatted correctly and prepped in the same software the venue runs (almost always Rekordbox on Pioneer CDJs). A third stick — or your phone with a portable library — is your deep-backup. Use quality drives (SanDisk Extreme, Samsung) of 64-128GB; cheap drives read slowly and corrupt under heat. Always FAT32 or exFAT, never NTFS or Mac-only HFS+, or the CDJ won't read it.

Export, then eject properly. A USB pulled mid-write becomes a corrupt database that shows zero tracks on the CDJ even though files are there. Export, wait, eject through the OS, then re-insert and verify it loads on a real CDJ or in Rekordbox export mode before you leave home.

What goes on every stick

  • Your full gig playlist plus 2-3 backup playlists (warm-up, peak, curveball) so you can pivot if the room is different than briefed.
  • Analysed tracks with set beatgrids, hot cues, and memory cues — never rely on the booth CDJ to analyse on the fly.
  • A handful of universal 'rescue' tracks: big, safe, crowd-pleasing records that work in almost any room when you need to buy time.

The physical kit bag

ItemWhy it saves the night
2x prepped USBs + 1 backupDrive failure or a stick left in a CDJ at the last club
Own headphones + 3.5mm-to-6.35mm adapterBooth headphones are often broken or filthy
RCA cables + a 3.5mm aux adapterFor laptop/controller hookup if the house feed is dead
USB-C/Lightning adapters, USB hubModern laptops lack ports; venues have old USB-A
Gaff tape, sharpie, ear plugsTaping cables, labelling, protecting your hearing
Phone with offline mix + power bankAbsolute last-resort music source

The rider

Your technical rider is a one-page document you send the promoter in advance. Keep it realistic for the venue size. A working DJ rider specifies: 2-3 working CDJs (state the model — CDJ-2000NXS2, CDJ-3000) and a DJM mixer, a flat USB hub if you bring a controller, a sturdy table at the right height, a monitor wedge you can actually hear, and basic hospitality (water, towels). Don't demand 4x CDJ-3000s for a 200-cap bar; you'll just get ignored.

Contingency planning

Before the gig, answer three questions in writing to yourself: What if my main USB fails? (Insert backup into the other deck and keep going.) What if the booth has gear I've never touched? (Watch a model-specific walkthrough the night before — a CDJ-3000 menu differs from a CDJ-900.) What if the set time changes? (Have a warm-up and a peak playlist ready so you can be flexible.) Confirm set time, slot, and load-in with the promoter 24-48 hours out, and screenshot the reply.

Arrive prepped, not packing. Building crates in the green room is amateur hour. Your selection work (see selection-5) is done before you leave; on-site you only adapt, never assemble.
exercise: Build your gig kit and test it cold. Export your gig playlist to two USB sticks formatted exFAT, eject properly, and confirm both load fully on a CDJ or in Rekordbox export mode. Then write a three-line contingency note answering what you do if (a) your main USB dies, (b) the booth gear is unfamiliar, and (c) your slot moves earlier.

tracks.title: Music Sounds Better with You
tracks.why: A universal rescue record — instantly lifts almost any room, ideal as a safe backup track on every gig stick.

title: Arriving, Booth Etiquette & Smooth Changeovers
skill: Handle booth etiquette and swap in and out of a live set with the previous DJ without dropping the energy.
content:
How you behave in the booth is your reputation

Promoters rebook DJs who are easy to work with as much as ones who play well. Arrive early — at least 30 minutes before your slot, more for a bigger room — sober enough to think, and respectful of the person currently playing. The booth is a workspace, not a hangout.

The golden rules of booth etiquette

  • Never touch the playing DJ's gear, mixer, or laptop. Don't lean on the table or set drinks near the CDJs.
  • Don't request your free deck until you genuinely need it to cue up — and ask first with a gesture or quiet word.
  • Keep your guests out of the booth. A crowded booth gets cables kicked and tracks knocked off-beat.
  • Wait for a natural break to introduce yourself; don't talk into the outgoing DJ's ear during a tricky mix.
  • Match, don't crash. Continue the energy and genre the room is already in — your set starts where theirs ends, not where your ego wants to begin.
Never drinks above the gear. A spilled beer into a DJM is a four-figure repair and an instantly dead changeover. Keep all liquids below the table line, full stop.

Anatomy of a clean changeover

On a standard 4-channel DJM the outgoing DJ usually uses channels 1 and 2; you set up on 3 and 4 (or whichever pair is free). This lets both of you have decks live simultaneously so the music never stops.

StepAction
1. Set up quietlyInsert your USB in a free deck, load your first track, set channel fader down and trim to match levels
2. Match level & gainCheck your channel's meter peaks the same as theirs so the swap isn't a volume jump
3. Beatmatch the handoverPre-PFL your incoming track in headphones, beatmatch and phrase-match to the outgoing track
4. Blend inBring your fader up, EQ-swap the bass, the previous DJ pulls theirs down over a phrase
5. Take the roomOnce you're solo on the master, settle, breathe, and start steering

When there's only two decks

Small bars often have a 2-channel mixer with both decks already in use. Agree a plan: the outgoing DJ ends on a clean outro, drops the fader, and you start fresh on the now-free deck. A two-second gap is fine and far better than a train wreck. Confirm with a quick word: 'Want me to mix in on your last track, or take it from a fresh drop?'

Reading the handover energy

Check the room as you arrive — not the dancefloor you wish for, the one in front of you. If the previous DJ has it peaking and you're the peak act, ride it. If they've over-cooked it and the floor is gassed out, you may need to ease off two notches and rebuild. Don't fight the room you inherit; manage it.

Thank the DJ, on and off the mic. A nod, a handshake, and naming them is free goodwill that gets you spoken well of. Scene reputation is built one polite changeover at a time.
exercise: Practice a live-to-live changeover with a friend or recording. Set up on the free channel pair while a track is playing, match gain so the meters read level, beatmatch your incoming track in headphones, then blend in over a 16-32 bar phrase while the outgoing track is pulled down. The goal is zero volume jump and zero silence.

tracks.artist: Roy Davis Jr. feat. Peven Everett

title: Soundcheck & Working with the Sound Engineer
skill: Run a soundcheck and communicate with the engineer to dial in monitors and main levels.
content:
The engineer is your most important ally

The front-of-house (FOH) engineer controls what the room hears and what you hear in the monitors. Treat them with respect, learn their name, and speak their language, and they'll make you sound enormous. Antagonise them — or worse, ride the booth gain trying to fix the room yourself — and you'll fight bad sound all night.

What soundcheck is actually for

Soundcheck is to set two things: your source level into the system (gain structure) and your monitoring (what you hear to mix). It is not the time to test every track or play a mini-set. Bring one or two tracks you know intimately — ideally one bass-heavy and one with vocals — so you can judge the system honestly.

Gain structure, from your hands to the speakers

  1. Set your channel trim/gain so the channel meter peaks around the top of green into the first amber segment on the loudest part of the track — never pinning red.
  2. Keep the master out of the red; leave headroom for the limiter the engineer has on the system.
  3. Set channel faders near the top and master around unity, then let FOH set the room volume. You control mix balance; they control room loudness.
Don't fix the room with booth gain. If it's too quiet out front, ask the engineer to bring up FOH — don't crank your master into the limiter. Redlining your output just makes the whole PA distort and ruins your dynamics.

Monitors: hearing yourself to mix

You cannot beatmatch or judge a blend off a muddy room reflection. You need a clear monitor source. Options, in order of how much control you want:

MonitoringBest forWatch out for
Booth wedge monitorClubs; quick to set upFeedback, time-smear vs FOH, often too quiet
Headphones (split cue)Loud or echoey roomsEar fatigue; isolates you from the room
In-ear monitors (IEMs)Festivals, big stagesNeeds the engineer to feed your monitor mix

Talking to the engineer

Use clear, specific, non-emotional requests. Good phrasing gets results:

  • 'Can I get more of my channel in the booth monitor?' (not 'it sounds bad')
  • 'A touch more low-mid in the wedge, around 200-300 Hz.'
  • 'The monitor's feeding back — can we pull a little around 2k?'
  • 'What's my headroom before the system limiter kicks in?'

Set the monitor loud enough to mix confidently but no louder — every dB in the wedge costs your ears over a long night, and over-loud monitors bleed into FOH. If you're on headphones, use split-cue so you hear the cued track in one ear and the master in the other, and set the booth/master balance knob so you're hearing enough of the live mix.

The two-minute pre-set check

Even with no formal soundcheck, do a silent one as you take over: confirm your channel is on the right input, trim set, headphones working, monitor audible, and the cue button lights up. Five seconds of checking prevents the classic disaster of pushing up a fader to silence because the USB was in the wrong deck.
exercise: Run a structured soundcheck on any system. Load a bass-heavy track you know, set channel trim so it peaks at green-into-amber with the master out of the red, then dial your monitor or split-cue headphones until you can clearly hear the beat to mix. Write down one specific request you'd make to an engineer to improve your monitor.

tracks.title: Spastik
tracks.why: A stripped, percussive techno tool with huge dynamics and deep bass — ideal for judging gain structure and how a monitor reproduces low end.

title: The Craft of a Warm-Up Set
skill: Play a patient warm-up set that builds the room and sets up the headliner instead of peaking early.
content:
The hardest, most respected slot

Anyone can drop bangers to a full room at midnight. Reading a half-empty room at 10pm and patiently building it so the headliner walks into a primed dancefloor — that's a craft, and it's what gets you rebooked and respected by bigger acts. The warm-up DJ's job is service, not showing off.

The cardinal rule: don't peak early

Your ceiling is set by your slot, not your ego. If you're on at 9-11pm before a 1am headline, you should leave the room wanting more energy, not exhausted. A common failure is the warm-up DJ playing their best peak-time records two hours early — now the headliner has to either go even harder (impossible) or the energy sags. Hold material in reserve.

DimensionWarm-up targetWhy
BPMLower / slower (e.g. 118-122 for house)Leaves room to climb later
EnergyGroove over impact; deep, dubby, melodicSets atmosphere, not a frenzy
Vocals/hooksSparse, atmosphericSave the sing-along anthems for peak
Mixing styleLong, smooth blendsContinuity over flashy tricks
Track for the room you have, not the one you want. Six people at the bar don't need a drop — they need a reason to drift toward the floor. Warm, rolling grooves at conversation-friendly energy pull people in; a premature anthem empties the room.

Building an arc

Think of your set as a gentle ramp. Open low and spacious, establish a groove, and raise energy in small, deliberate steps — a slightly busier record, a few BPM more, a touch more bass — across the whole slot. By your last 15 minutes you hand over at a point that the headliner can take and lift. Plan your handover BPM and energy to dovetail with what you know the next DJ opens on.

Practical selection tactics

  • Favour records with long intros and outros for unhurried blends.
  • Use deeper, lesser-known cuts — the warm-up is where digging pays off and you set a tasteful tone.
  • Keep dynamics: a stripped, hypnotic record makes the next, fuller one feel like a lift even at low overall energy.
  • Mind the key journey (harmonic mixing) so the room feels coherent and hypnotic rather than jarring.

Reading the early room

Watch feet and shoulders, not just whether the floor is full. People nodding, drifting closer, settling in — that's success. If the floor thins, you've pushed too hard or too odd; pull back to a warmer, simpler groove. If they're locked in and you still have time, resist the urge to cash it in early — bank that energy.

Ego management

You will not get the screaming peak moment tonight, and that's the point. The promoter and headliner notice the DJ who left the room perfectly poised. That reputation — 'great warm-up, easy to work with, reads a room' — is how warm-up DJs become headliners.

Hand over, don't slam the door. End on a record that flows into the headliner's vibe and tempo. A warm-up that climaxes on its biggest track sabotages the act it's supposed to set up.
exercise: Record a 30-minute warm-up set to an empty room. Start around 118-120 BPM with deep, groove-led tracks and long blends, then raise energy in small steps so the final track is clearly more energetic than the first but still below peak. Listen back and check you never 'spent' a true anthem — if you did, swap it for something deeper.

tracks.title: At Les
tracks.why: A patient, building Detroit groove that rises without ever peaking — a masterclass in warm-up restraint and slow energy climb.

title: Peak-Time Performance, Energy & Stagecraft
skill: Command a peak-time slot with high-energy selection and stagecraft that connects with the crowd.
content:
Peak time is about command, not just bangers

At peak the room is full, primed, and expecting you to take charge. Your job is to convert that potential into a shared, memorable experience — to give the crowd moments they'll talk about tomorrow. That takes both selection and presence.

Energy management at the top

You can't simply play loud bangers back to back for 90 minutes — the ear normalises and everything flattens. Peak energy is created by contrast. Pull back, then surge. A breakdown, a stripped groove, or a vocal-only moment makes the next drop hit twice as hard. Think of energy as a series of waves cresting higher, not a flat ceiling.

ToolEffect on the floor
Build / breakdown then dropTension and release — the core dancefloor payoff
Double drop (see advanced-7)A huge, signature peak moment when timed on the phrase
Acapella over a beatRecognition spike — the crowd sings, hands go up
Filter/FX tension buildLifts the room before a big record
A track everyone knowsMass sing-along; the rare safe 'cheat code' anthem
Mix the floor, not the headphones. At peak, technical perfection matters less than energy and timing. A slightly loose blend that lands a huge record on the downbeat beats a flawless mix into a track nobody reacts to. Watch the room more than the gear.

Stagecraft: connecting with the crowd

Presence is performance. The crowd feeds off your body language, so give them something to mirror:

  • Look up. Make eye contact, point at people, react when they react. A DJ staring at a laptop kills the room's energy.
  • Use your hands to cue the crowd before a drop — the raised arm, the count-in. They'll throw their hands with you.
  • Move with the music. Genuine enthusiasm is contagious; performative flailing is not — find your honest version.
  • Use the mic sparingly and only with purpose — a single 'make some noise' before a drop, never constant chatter.

Building and landing the big moment

Plan one or two signature moments per set — the record that's yours tonight, set up with a long tension build so the drop lands as a release. Read the floor (selection-2) and seize it when the room is ripe (selection-6); a perfectly timed anthem at the right second is worth ten well-mixed records. Don't blow all your ammunition in the first ten minutes — pace your biggest records so the set keeps escalating.

Holding the peak without exhausting it

Even at peak, you need dynamics. If you've been flat-out for 20 minutes, drop to a hypnotic, driving groove for a few minutes so the next surge feels new. Watch for the room overheating — if hands drop and people head for the bar, you've over-saturated; give them a breather track, then rebuild. Sustained peak is a heartbeat, not a held note.

End on a high, then get off. Finish your slot on a defining record at full energy and hand over cleanly. Overstaying or fading out limply erases the moment you just built.
exercise: Build and record a 20-minute peak sequence with one signature moment. Construct a clear energy wave: a stripped groove, a tension build, then a big anthem dropped exactly on the phrase downbeat. Film yourself and check your stagecraft — are you looking up and cueing the crowd, or buried in the screen?

tracks.title: Losing It
tracks.why: A relentless, build-and-release peak-time weapon — perfect for practicing tension builds, a massive drop, and timing the crowd's hands-up moment.

title: Festival & Big-Stage Specifics: Pro-Link, IEMs, Timecode & Visuals
skill: Play a big festival stage using CDJ pro-link, in-ears, timecode and cueing the LD/visuals within strict set times.
content:
A festival stage is a different machine

Big stages are tightly run productions with stage managers, FOH and monitor engineers, a lighting designer (LD), and a visuals/VJ operator. You are one part of a synchronised show on a hard clock. The technical craft is similar to a club, but the margins for error and the rigidity of timing are far stricter.

CDJ Pro DJ Link (pro-link)

Pro DJ Link is the Ethernet network that connects the CDJs and DJM together. It enables features you'll rely on at festival scale:

  • One USB, multiple players: a single USB in one CDJ can be browsed and loaded across all linked players — so you only need one prepped stick live (still bring backups).
  • Beat sync / Link cues: shared beat grid and quantised cueing across decks.
  • Master tempo & phase info shared so the rig behaves as one instrument.
Verify the link in soundcheck. Confirm the CDJs show 'LINK' and your USB browses across all decks before doors. A pro-link that isn't talking means you're stuck loading from one player — discover that now, not mid-set in front of 10,000 people.

In-ear monitors (IEMs)

On a big stage, wedge monitors can't compete with the volume and time-delay of a massive PA bouncing off the field. IEMs give you an isolated, clean monitor mix fed by the monitor engineer. Expect a wired pack (or a wireless belt-pack) with your own mix — usually your master plus a little crowd mic so you don't feel disconnected. Bring your own moulded in-ears if you have them. Run one ear in, one out if you want to feel the room, but mix off the IEM, not the field echo. Tell the monitor engineer exactly what you want in the mix: 'master, a touch of crowd, no FOH delay.'

Timecode and set times

'Timecode' means two different things at festivals; know both:

TermWhat it meansYour job
Set time / stage clockYour exact on/off times, often locked to a broadcast or curfewStart on time, end on time, to the minute
SMPTE/MIDI timecode showPre-programmed light/visual/pyro shows synced to a timelineStay locked to the planned track order so cues hit
DVS timecode (control vinyl)Software control if you're on a turntable/DVS rigCalibrate signal at soundcheck

Set times are sacred. Going over eats into the next act and can trip a noise curfew that fines the promoter — a fast way to never get rebooked. Have a visible clock or count it on your IEM cue. Plan an ending you can reach a few minutes early and stretch or cut, so you land exactly on time.

Cueing the LD and visuals

The LD and VJ are reading the music and you — give them signals so the production lands with your drops:

  • Agree hand signals beforehand: a raised fist or count-down fingers before a drop tells the LD to hit the strobe/blackout-to-bang.
  • If your set is on a fixed timeline (pre-programmed show), you must keep your track order, because lights and pyro fire on the clock, not your decks.
  • Use clear body language on the build — the LD lights the build, blacks out, and slams on your drop. Sloose timing makes them miss it.

Prep that scales

Everything from lesson performance-1 still applies, harder. Rehearse the set if it's timed to a show. Pre-export to a single pro-link-ready USB plus backups. Confirm your rider matches the stage's installed rig (CDJ-3000 + DJM-V10/900NXS2 is common). Build in 60-90 seconds of flex at the end so you hit your off-time even if a transition runs long. A recorded version of this set is also prime content for your mixes/EPK (brand-3).
exercise: Plan a strictly timed 30-minute festival set to a fixed clock. Write a track-by-track timeline with running times so you land exactly at 30:00, mark where you'd give the LD a drop signal, and note your IEM monitor request. Then perform it once, watching a clock, and adjust your final track so you can hit the off-time to within ten seconds.

tracks.title: Opus
tracks.why: A long, programmatic build-and-drop designed for big-stage light shows — perfect for rehearsing LD cue signals and tight set-time planning.

title: Disaster Recovery & B2B Sets
skill: Recover instantly from needle skips, power cuts and laptop crashes, and run a smooth back-to-back set.
content:
The crowd remembers how you recovered, not that it broke

Gear fails on everyone. What separates pros is the calm, instant response. The worst thing you can do is freeze, look panicked, or grab the mic to apologise. Stay composed, fix it, and most of the room never realises anything happened.

Common disasters and the instant fix

DisasterInstant response
Needle skip / CDJ track jumpCut that channel's fader, re-cue or jump to a hot cue on the beat, fade back in on the phrase
Bumped jog / lost beatmatchNudge back into phase by ear; if it's gone, cut the channel and re-drop on the next downbeat
Laptop crash (controller/Serato)Switch to USB/CDJ if available; otherwise relaunch software while the other deck holds the floor
USB read errorEject, re-seat, or pull your backup stick into the free deck and keep the music going
Power cut / system muteStay calm, don't touch master gain; when it returns, ease the level up, don't slam it
Sound cuts out one channelSwap to the other deck/channel; check cable and input selector
Always have a record running you can hide behind. The single best disaster insurance is to never be fully committed to one deck. Keep the outgoing track playable a little longer so that if the incoming one fails, you fall back instead of falling into silence.

The 'buy time' move

When something breaks and you need three seconds to think: loop the currently playing track. A 4 or 8-beat loop on the live deck holds the groove indefinitely while you fix the broken deck, swap a USB, or relaunch software. Loop, fix, exit the loop on the phrase. The crowd hears a slightly extended section, not a crisis.

Preventing disasters

  • Backups on a second USB (performance-1) turn a USB failure into a five-second swap.
  • Don't lean on the booth or stack drinks near gear — most 'disasters' are kicked cables and spills.
  • Check your master isn't pinned into the limiter so a surge doesn't cut the system.
  • Know the gear's recovery: where the hot cues are, how to reload a track, how to eject and re-read a USB on that exact CDJ model.

Back-to-back (B2B) sets

A B2B is two (or more) DJs sharing one set, usually trading every 1-2 tracks. Done well it's electric; done badly it's two people fighting over the mixer. The key is communication and ego-checking.

How to run a clean B2B

  1. Agree the pattern up front: one track each, two each, or whoever's hot keeps going. Know who's loading the next track on which deck.
  2. Build on each other: respond to what your partner just played — match or lift the energy, follow the key and tempo. It's a conversation, not a contest.
  3. Hand over cleanly: the person who just mixed in leaves their deck playing and steps back; the other loads the free deck and takes the next mix. Don't both grab the EQ.
  4. Communicate constantly: point to the deck you're loading, signal your BPM, agree who handles a drop. A quick word or hand sign prevents two people mixing at once.
B2B is generosity, not a battle. The best B2B DJs make their partner sound great and read each other like a band. Don't sabotage with a hard genre swerve or hog the mixer — the audience can feel cooperation versus competition.

Mindset under pressure

Whether it's a crash or a chaotic B2B, the principle is the same: stay calm, keep one thing playing, and solve the next ten seconds. Panic is contagious and so is composure — choose composure.
exercise: Rehearse a recovery and a B2B handover. First, while a track plays, simulate a failed incoming deck: drop a 4-beat loop on the live track, 'fix' for a few seconds, then exit the loop cleanly on the phrase. Then with a partner (or by alternating yourself), run a two-track-each B2B where each new track matches or lifts the previous one's energy and key.

tracks.title: Percolator
tracks.why: A loopable, groove-locked track that's easy to hold on a loop to buy time, and a friendly, energy-flexible record for trading in a B2B.
